sentence: Tricyclic antidepressants are a group of medicines that includes amitriptyline, nortriptyline, imipramine and clomipramine.
note: StatPearls TCA; NHS nortriptyline; MedlinePlus clomipramine

sentence: They are used to treat depression, and amitriptyline and nortriptyline are also used for pain relief at lower doses than for depression.
They cause more significant side effects than many newer antidepressants, and they are more dangerous when taken in overdose.
note: StatPearls: more significant adverse effects due to anticholinergic activity and lower threshold for overdose

sentence: Their main action is blocking the reuptake of noradrenaline and serotonin.
The NHS says they are thought to work by increasing levels of serotonin in the brain.
Many of their side effects come from anticholinergic activity.
For imipramine, StatPearls lists blurred vision, constipation, a fast heartbeat, confusion, dry mouth and urinary retention among these effects.
A 2024 review concluded that, with one exception, all tricyclics are toxic and dangerous when taken in overdose.
The exception named in that review is lofepramine, a tricyclic used in the UK.
Cardiac arrhythmia is the leading cause of death in tricyclic antidepressant overdose.

Overdose is serious: anyone who has taken more than the prescribed amount and has a fast or irregular heartbeat, a seizure, drowsiness or passing out, difficulty breathing or sudden confusion needs a 999 call.
Some local NHS prescribing guidance advises limiting the amount prescribed each time because of the risk of toxicity in overdose.
Clomipramine carries a boxed warning in the US about increased suicidal thinking in young people.
The NHS says to call 999 or go to A&E now for thoughts of harming yourself or ending your life; NHS 111 is open 24 hours every day and Samaritans is a free line on 116 123.
The NHS says it can be dangerous to take amitriptyline with methadone, stimulants such as MDMA or cocaine, hallucinogens such as LSD, and some new psychoactive substances.
Taking more than the prescribed amount can cause serious effects such as a change in heartbeat and seizures (fits); the NHS says to call 999 now if symptoms follow and to contact NHS 111 for advice.
